summary.title: The 7 Most Influential Papers in Computer Science History
summary.one_liner: A subjective, chronological tour of seven foundational CS papers (Turing, Shannon, Codd, Cook, Cerf and Kahn, Berners-Lee, Brin and Page) and why each still shapes modern computing, plus five honorable mentions.
keywords: attention is all you need transformer
takeaways: Turing's 1936 paper defined the Turing machine and the limits of what is computable.
Shannon (1948), Codd (1970), Cook (1971), Cerf and Kahn (1974) laid groundwork for information theory, relational databases, NP-completeness, and TCP/IP.
Berners-Lee's 1989 proposal led to the World Wide Web; Brin and Page's 1998 paper introduced PageRank behind Google.
Five bonus papers (McCarthy's Lisp, Dijkstra's goto, Lamport's clocks, Brooks' No Silver Bullet, and the Transformer paper) are also highlighted.
summary.summary: The author presents a subjective list of seven papers in computer science history, sorted by date, chosen mainly for their impact on today's technology. Each entry gives the paper's core idea, why it matters now, and links to the original PDF, a Wikipedia page, or a video. The post closes with five bonus papers that narrowly missed the main list, each with a short explanation, and a concluding note on the value of understanding foundations.
